alt: An appliance with a metal case. Current flows in through the live wire, which contains the fuse, through the heating element and back through the neutral wire. The earth wire joins the metal case to the ground and carries no current in normal use.
caption: Live in, neutral back; the earth wire carries current only when there is a fault.

alt: Three steps. The live wire touches the metal case. A large current flows through the case and the low-resistance earth wire to the ground rather than through a person. The large current melts the fuse, disconnecting the live wire.
caption: Earthing gives the fault current an easy path, and that large current blows the fuse.

alt: Double insulation: live parts inside an insulating case, with the square-in-a-square symbol and no earth wire. A fuse melts when the current is too large and must be replaced; a circuit breaker trips open and can be reset. Both go in the live side.
caption: Each safety feature protects in its own way; fuses and breakers always go in the live wire.

after: ## Why a current heats a resistor (2.3)
alt: Electrons drifting through a metal resistor collide with the positive ions of the metal and transfer energy to them, so the ions vibrate more and the temperature rises. This is useful in heating elements and fuses and wasteful in cables.
caption: Electron–ion collisions make the ions vibrate more: electrical energy becomes thermal energy.

alt: Two number lines with 3 A, 5 A and 13 A fuses. A 1.4 kW, 230 V hairdryer takes 6.1 A, so the 13 A fuse is chosen. A 60 W, 230 V lamp takes 0.26 A, so the 3 A fuse is chosen.
caption: Work out I = P ÷ V, then pick the smallest fuse rating above it.

alt: A heater takes 8.7 A from 230 V for 2.0 hours. The time is 7200 s, so E = 8.7 × 230 × 7200 = 14 407 200 J, about 1.4 × 10⁷ J.
caption: Convert hours to seconds, then E = I × V × t.

alt: Two voltage–time graphs. d.c. from a cell or battery is a horizontal line. a.c. from the mains is a wave that goes positive, then negative, then positive again.
caption: d.c. flows one way; mains a.c. keeps reversing direction.
